title: Smoking, alcohol and substance use
blurb: Test CO, make the opt-out referral, give clear alcohol advice and open the right pathway when a woman discloses substance use.
question: Kayleigh, 24, is at her booking appointment at 9 weeks. Her carbon monoxide (CO) reading is 6 ppm and she says she has 'nearly stopped' smoking. She also asks whether the odd glass of wine is fine. What should the midwife do and say?

teach.h: Why the midwife asks every woman
teach.body: Smoking, alcohol and drug use in pregnancy are among the most changeable causes of harm to babies. NICE NG201 asks midwives to discuss smoking, recreational drugs and alcohol at booking and later 'in a non-judgemental, compassionate and personalised way'. In plain English: ask everyone, measure what you can (carbon monoxide), give one clear message, and make referral the default rather than something the woman has to request.

A high reading in a woman who does not smoke may mean a faulty boiler or appliance: advise on CO poisoning and the Gas Emergency Line (NICE NG209).

teach.body: NG201 says to explain that there is no known safe level of alcohol in pregnancy, that drinking can cause long-term harm to the baby, and that the safest approach is to avoid alcohol altogether. The adult '14 units a week' low-risk guideline does not apply in pregnancy. Give the message kindly and without judgement, and offer support if she finds it hard to stop.

teach.body: Kayleigh's CO is 6 ppm and she still smokes, so the midwife explains the reading kindly and makes an opt-out referral to the in-house adviser today, mentioning NRT and voucher support. Her partner also smokes, so he is offered referral too (NG201 1.2.4). On wine, the midwife says there is no known safe level and the safest choice is none. Everything is recorded, and her CO will be repeated at 36 weeks.

teach.text: 'Cutting down' is not stopping. Any woman who smokes, has quit in the last 2 weeks or reads 4 ppm or more gets the opt-out referral now: do not wait for her to ask, and do not wait for the 36-week test. And a high reading in a non-smoker is a carbon monoxide safety problem, not a smoking problem.

items: Offer every woman a CO test at booking and at 36 weeks (SBL v3 element 1).
Smoker, quit within 2 weeks, or 4 ppm or more: opt-out referral to the tobacco dependence adviser.
NRT is the medicine to use in pregnancy (patches off at bedtime); not varenicline, bupropion or cytisinicline.
Alcohol: no known safe level; the safest approach is to avoid it altogether.
Substance use: offer referral to a substance misuse programme at first disclosure, a named specialist midwife or doctor, and multi-agency planning.

summary: You can now run the SBL v3 smoking pathway from CO test to opt-out referral and NRT, give NICE's alcohol message without hedging, and start the CG110 pathway when a woman discloses substance use. You can also spot a non-smoker whose high CO reading signals a carbon monoxide hazard.

A.q: At booking, Kayleigh's CO reading is 6 ppm. She says she has 'nearly stopped' and is down to three cigarettes a day. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Repeat the CO test at 36 weeks before referring
Make an opt-out referral to the tobacco adviser
Give a leaflet and ask her to self-refer when ready
Ask the GP to prescribe varenicline for her
A.why: SBL v3 element 1: a CO reading of 4 ppm or more, or any self-identified smoker, should be referred on an opt-out basis to the in-house tobacco dependence adviser now.

whyNot.0: The 36-week test is a second routine check, not a reason to delay referral for a woman who smokes today.
whyNot.2: Self-referral is the old model; SBL v3 makes referral the default, which she can decline.
whyNot.3: Varenicline is not used in pregnancy or breastfeeding (NICE NG209).

A.q: Under Saving Babies' Lives v3, at which antenatal contacts should a CO test be offered to every pregnant woman?
options: At the dating scan and at 28 weeks
At booking and at 28 weeks
At booking and at 36 weeks
At booking and at the anomaly scan
A.why: SBL v3 element 1 asks for CO testing for all women at booking and at the 36-week appointment, and at other appointments for groups named in NICE NG209.

whyNot.0: Scans are not the SBL v3 CO-testing points; booking and 36 weeks are.
whyNot.1: 28 weeks is the anti-D and bloods appointment; the second routine CO test is at 36 weeks.
whyNot.3: The anomaly scan is not a CO-testing point.

A.q: A woman at 10 weeks asks how much wine she can safely drink while pregnant. Which response reflects NICE NG201?
options: Up to 14 units a week, spread over 3 days, is low risk
One or two units once a week is safe after 12 weeks
Small amounts are safe if she avoided it until now
There is no known safe level; avoiding alcohol is safest
A.why: NG201 1.3.10: there is no known safe level of alcohol in pregnancy, drinking can cause long-term harm to the baby, and the safest approach is to avoid alcohol altogether.

whyNot.0: 14 units a week is the CMO low-risk guideline for non-pregnant adults; it does not apply in pregnancy.
whyNot.1: This was older advice; current NICE guidance gives no 'safe' amount at any gestation.
whyNot.2: There is no safe amount whatever she drank earlier; the advice is to avoid alcohol.

B.q: Amira, 30, is 14 weeks pregnant and smokes 10 cigarettes a day. She wants a medicine to help her stop. Which option is appropriate in pregnancy?
options: Nicotine replacement, with patches off at bedtime
Varenicline, with weekly adviser follow-up
Bupropion, as it contains no nicotine
Cytisinicline, as it is plant-derived
B.why: NICE NG209 1.20.6, 1.20.7 and 1.20.9: consider NRT alongside behavioural support at the earliest opportunity in pregnancy, and advise women using patches to remove them before going to bed.

whyNot.1: Varenicline is not recommended in pregnancy or breastfeeding.
whyNot.2: Bupropion is not recommended in pregnancy or breastfeeding, whatever its nicotine content.
whyNot.3: Cytisinicline is not recommended in pregnancy or breastfeeding.

B.q: Aisha has never smoked and lives with a non-smoking partner. Her CO reading at booking is 12 ppm. What should the midwife do first?
options: Make an opt-out referral to stop-smoking services
Give CO poisoning advice and the Gas Emergency Line
Record it as a faulty reading and retest at 36 weeks
Ask her partner to come in for his own CO test
B.why: NICE NG209: a reading over 10 ppm in a woman who does not smoke suggests carbon monoxide exposure; give CO poisoning advice and the Gas Emergency Line number.

whyNot.0: She does not smoke, so a stop-smoking referral does not address the likely hazard at home.
whyNot.2: Dismissing the reading leaves her and her baby exposed to a possible CO leak for months.
whyNot.3: Her partner does not smoke either; the urgent issue is a possible faulty appliance.

B.q: At her first contact, Leanne tells the midwife she is pregnant and uses heroin daily. She is not in any treatment. According to NICE CG110, what should be offered?
options: A plan to book once her drug use is stable
A leaflet, with a review at the 16-week visit
Referral to a substance misuse programme
A discussion of her use with her partner
B.why: CG110 1.2.7: the first time a woman who misuses substances discloses she is pregnant, offer referral to an appropriate substance misuse programme.

whyNot.0: Delaying booking adds a barrier; she needs antenatal care and treatment together now.
whyNot.1: CG110 asks for referral at first disclosure, not a wait until 16 weeks.
whyNot.3: Her disclosure is confidential to her; involving her partner is her choice, not the clinical response.

C.q: At 36 weeks, Kayleigh's CO reading is 5 ppm. She used NRT patches after her booking referral but now smokes 'a couple' a day. She plans to bed-share with her baby. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Advise that bed-sharing is safe if she smokes outdoors
Postpone further support until after the birth
Re-refer for support and advise against bed-sharing
Repeat the CO test at the six-week postnatal check
C.why: She is still smoking (5 ppm), so she should be re-referred for support. NICE NG194 1.3.15: strongly advise parents not to bed-share if either parent smokes.

whyNot.0: NG194 advises against bed-sharing when either parent smokes, wherever the smoking happens.
whyNot.1: Support should continue now; stopping before birth still benefits the baby.
whyNot.3: Waiting for a postnatal test misses the chance to act before the birth.

C.q: Grace does not smoke and her CO reading is 2 ppm, but her partner smokes 20 a day in the house. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Offer her partner referral to stop-smoking services
Make an opt-out referral for Grace herself
Record a normal reading and take no further action
Prescribe NRT to Grace to offset passive smoking
C.why: NICE NG201 1.2.4: if the woman or her partner smokes, offer a referral to NHS Stop Smoking Services. Second-hand smoke harms her and the baby.

whyNot.1: Grace is a non-smoker below 4 ppm, so the opt-out referral criteria for her are not met.
whyNot.2: Her partner's smoking is a modifiable risk that NG201 asks you to act on.
whyNot.3: NRT treats nicotine dependence in a smoker; it does nothing for passive exposure.

C.q: At 20 weeks, Maria discloses that she drinks a bottle of wine most nights. She wants help but is frightened her baby will be taken. Which response is best?
options: Promise her the disclosure will stay between the two of them
Advise cutting down to 14 units a week as a safer target
Note it and review her drinking at the 28-week appointment
Offer referral to alcohol services and explain how agencies help
C.why: CG110: offer referral to a substance misuse programme and address her fears about children's services with honest, tailored information (1.2.1, 1.2.7). She must also be told why and when information may be shared (1.1.9).

whyNot.0: Midwives cannot promise secrecy; information may need sharing to safeguard her baby (CG110 1.1.9).
whyNot.1: There is no known safe level of alcohol in pregnancy; 14 units is the non-pregnant guideline.
whyNot.2: Waiting 8 weeks delays treatment for a woman who has asked for help today.

reteach.title: Ask, test, refer, support
reteach.question: Think of the pathway as four verbs. Which one do midwives most often skip?

blocks.body: Ask every woman about smoking, alcohol and drugs. Test CO at booking and 36 weeks. Refer anyone who smokes, quit within 2 weeks or reads 4 ppm or more, on an opt-out basis. Support with behavioural help, NRT and incentives. The step most often missed is 'refer': SBL v3 makes it automatic unless she declines.

blocks.text: Alcohol has no 'safe' amount in pregnancy. The 14-units-a-week figure is the adult guideline outside pregnancy and is the commonest wrong answer.

explain.body: Every woman is offered a CO test at booking and 36 weeks. A reading of 4 ppm or more, a self-identified smoker, or someone who stopped in the last 2 weeks gets an opt-out referral to the in-house tobacco dependence adviser.

test.q: Which CO reading triggers an opt-out referral under SBL v3?
options: 2 ppm or above
4 ppm or above
7 ppm or above
10 ppm or above
test.why: SBL v3 element 1 sets the opt-out referral threshold at 4 ppm or above.

whyNot.2: 7 ppm is above it, but the trigger is lower, at 4 ppm.
whyNot.3: Over 10 ppm in a non-smoker prompts CO poisoning advice; the referral threshold is 4 ppm.

explain.body: NRT is considered at the earliest opportunity, alongside behavioural support. Patches are removed at bedtime. Varenicline, bupropion and cytisinicline are not used in pregnancy or breastfeeding.

test.q: Which advice about NRT patches in pregnancy is correct?
options: Wear them for 24 hours a day
Start them after 12 weeks
Remove them at bedtime
Combine them with varenicline
test.why: NICE NG209: pregnant women using nicotine patches should remove them before going to bed.

whyNot.0: Patches are taken off at bedtime in pregnancy.
whyNot.1: NICE says to consider NRT at the earliest opportunity in pregnancy, not to delay it.
whyNot.3: Varenicline is not used in pregnancy.

explain.body: There is no known safe level of alcohol in pregnancy. Drinking can cause long-term harm to the baby, so the safest approach is to avoid alcohol altogether (NG201 1.3.10).

items.label: units a week: adult guideline outside pregnancy

test.q: Which statement reflects NICE NG201 on alcohol in pregnancy?
options: Up to 14 units a week is low risk
No known safe level; avoid alcohol
Small amounts are safe after 12 weeks
Wine is safer than spirits in pregnancy
test.why: NG201 1.3.10: no known safe level; the safest approach is to avoid alcohol altogether.

whyNot.0: 14 units a week is the non-pregnant adult guideline.
whyNot.3: The type of drink does not change the advice.

explain.body: At first disclosure, offer referral to a substance misuse programme. Provide a named midwife or doctor with specialist knowledge, coordinate a multi-agency plan including safeguarding, and address fears about children's services honestly (CG110).

test.q: When should a woman who misuses substances first be offered referral to a substance misuse programme?
options: At the 20-week anomaly scan appointment
After a month without using any drugs
At the 28-week antenatal appointment
When she first discloses the pregnancy
test.why: CG110 1.2.7: the first time a woman who misuses substances discloses she is pregnant, offer referral.

whyNot.0: Waiting until 20 weeks loses months of treatment.
whyNot.1: Referral is not conditional on abstinence.
whyNot.2: 28 weeks is far too late; referral is offered at first disclosure.
